title: Money for Grade 2: Rupees and Paise Made Easy (with a Free Quiz)
meta_title: Money for Grade 2: Rupees and Paise + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach Grade 2 money the easy way: recognise rupees and paise, make amounts, add shop prices and find change, with a free 8-question quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: Coins and notes are the first maths a child actually holds in their hand. Here is how I teach Grade 2 money — rupees and paise, making amounts, shop totals and change — plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a seven-year-old a ₹20 note at the kirana shop and something clicks that no worksheet ever manages on its own. Money in Grade 2 — rupees and paise — is the first bit of maths children touch, count and spend for real, which is exactly why it sticks. In my experience teaching this age, the child who has actually paid for a ₹12 packet of biscuits and counted the change understands addition better than the one who has only filled boxes on a page. So the plan here is simple: coins and notes first, then making the same amount in different ways, then adding up a small shopping list, and finally the bit every parent asks about — working out the change.

You do not need a till or plastic play money. Real coins from the drawer and a few notes are far better, because the child recognises what they will actually use.

Money in Grade 2: rupees and paise

Start with the one fact everything else rests on: one rupee (₹1) is made of 100 paise. At this age I would not labour paise beyond that. Paise coins have almost vanished from real shops in India, and honestly most Grade 2 children will never hold a 50-paise coin. But the NCERT syllabus still expects them to know the relationship, and it quietly plants the idea of 100 — the same 100 they meet in place value. So teach it, mention that we mostly use rupees today, and move on.

The coins and notes a child will genuinely see are worth naming clearly.

  • Coins: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10
  • Notes: ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100 (and higher, but stop here for Grade 2)
  • Paise: 50 paise still appears in textbooks — show it once so the word is not a mystery

Reading a price tag

Prices in the shop are written with the rupee sign in front: ₹8, ₹15, ₹40. A child who can read the number can read the price. The only new thing is the little ₹ symbol, and children learn to spot it fast once they know it means ‘this much money’.

Making the same amount in different ways

This is the idea that turns coin-recognition into real understanding: the same amount can be built from different coins. Ask a child to make ₹10 and let them find every route. It is a small puzzle they enjoy.

AmountOne wayAnother way
₹5One ₹5 coin₹2 + ₹2 + ₹1
₹10One ₹10 coin₹5 + ₹2 + ₹2 + ₹1
₹15₹10 + ₹5₹5 + ₹5 + ₹5
₹20One ₹20 note₹10 + ₹5 + ₹5

Here is the counter-intuitive bit worth knowing: children often think a fistful of small coins is more than one big coin, simply because there are more pieces. Four ₹2 coins feel like more than one ₹10 note. Sorting coins into equal piles and swapping five ₹1 coins for one ₹5 coin fixes this quickly, and it is the seed of place value again — ten ones become one ten.

Adding up prices at the shop

Now the maths does real work. Picture a small kirana list: a pencil for ₹7, an eraser for ₹5, and a toffee for ₹3. Adding ₹7 + ₹5 + ₹3 is just Grade 2 addition wearing a rupee sign. I teach children to add the two that make a round number first — here ₹7 + ₹3 = ₹10 — then add the ₹5 to reach ₹15. Same trick they use with plain numbers, now with a reason to care about the answer.

Keep the totals under ₹100 and the individual prices small and real. A notebook for ₹25, a packet of chips for ₹10, a pen for ₹5 — these are prices a child recognises from actual shops, which matters more than you would think for keeping them interested.

Working out simple change

Change is where money maths feels grown-up, and it is nothing more than subtraction dressed up. If a chocolate costs ₹15 and you pay with a ₹20 note, the change is ₹20 − ₹15 = ₹5. The way shopkeepers actually do it — counting up from the price to the note — is also the gentler method for children: ‘fifteen… and five more makes twenty, so five rupees back.’

One honest caveat from the classroom: do not rush to big notes. A child who confidently gives change from a ₹20 note is ready; the same child handed a ₹100 note for a ₹35 purchase will freeze. Grow the numbers slowly. Change from ₹10, then from ₹20, then from ₹50 — in that order — and the skill builds without the panic.

A few mistakes to expect

These trip up almost every Grade 2 child, and none of them mean your child is behind:

  • Counting the number of coins instead of their value (three ₹1 coins read as ‘three rupees’, which is right, but three ₹5 coins read as ‘three rupees’ too).
  • Forgetting the rupee sign when writing a price.
  • Trying to give change by counting down instead of up.

Catch these early with real coins in hand, not corrections on paper, and they fade on their own.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz on exactly these skills — recognising coins, making amounts, adding shop prices and finding change. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for any they miss. quiz.title: Grade 2 Money Quiz: Rupees and Paise
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on coins, notes, making amounts, shop totals and change. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 2 Indian money — rupees and paise

questions.q: How many paise make one rupee (₹1)?
questions.explanation: One rupee is made of 100 paise. That is the same 100 you meet when counting in tens.

questions.q: Riya buys a pencil for ₹7 and an eraser for ₹5. What does she pay in all?
questions.explanation: ₹7 + ₹5 = ₹12. Adding the rupee sign does not change the addition.

questions.q: A chocolate costs ₹15. You pay with a ₹20 note. How much change do you get?
questions.explanation: Change is ₹20 − ₹15 = ₹5. Count up: fifteen and five more makes twenty.

questions.q: Which is more money, ₹50 or 50 paise?
questions.explanation: ₹50 is fifty rupees. 50 paise is only half a rupee, so ₹50 is much more.

questions.q: How can you make exactly ₹6 using coins?
A packet of biscuits costs ₹25. You give a ₹50 note. What is the change?
questions.explanation: ₹50 − ₹25 = ₹25. Twenty-five and twenty-five more makes fifty.

questions.q: Which set of coins makes exactly ₹15?

faq.q: What money skills should a Grade 2 child know?
faq.a: Recognising coins and notes up to ₹100, knowing that ₹1 is 100 paise, making an amount in different ways, adding a short list of prices, and working out simple change from ₹10 or ₹20.

faq.q: Do children still need to learn paise?
faq.a: The syllabus keeps it, so yes — a child should know one rupee is 100 paise. In real shops paise coins are almost gone, so I teach the fact once and spend the practice time on rupees.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to teach change?
faq.a: Count up from the price to the note rather than subtracting downwards. For a ₹15 item paid with ₹20, say ‘fifteen and five more makes twenty’ — that gives ₹5 change without any borrowing.

faq.q: Should I use real coins or play money?
faq.a: Real coins, every time. Children recognise the coins they will actually use, and the weight and size help them tell ₹2 from ₹5. Play money adds a step of pretend that this age does not need.
